title: Rain squall on the heather moor

tokens.v: Full-bleed, edge to edge, no border or letterbox band. A squall on a high moor in late August: no sun, flat silver light from the whole sky and nothing behind the jar, so the honey sits two stops under the sky — a near-opaque dark brown-amber mass, its only bright lines the meniscus at the shoulder and facet corners catching silver. The lid is turned solid oak: a tall straight-sided cylinder as deep as it is wide, softly rounded on top, no wider than the jar's shoulder, its fine parallel grain readable through the water film — wood, never cork, no porous mottle, clean glass below its skirt. The jar sits on a soaked granite slab, base flat to the stone with a hard dark contact line beneath it and no gap, owning half the frame. Bell heather is knocked flat all round, stems horizontal, all pointing downwind. One shutter throughout: rain reads as short bright streaks everywhere, including off the lid — no frozen droplets, no splash crown. 65mm at f/4 from just above slab height, the hill lost in rain-haze within twenty metres; heather runs out both side edges, the slab out the bottom.
